claim: CALHM2, CALHM4, and CALHM6 are highly expressed in human placental tissues.
source: By transcript analysis, we found the paralogs CALHM2, 4, and 6 to be highly expressed in this organ and upregulated during trophoblast differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data presented in Figure 1A showing high mRNA abundance of CALHM2, 4, and 6 in placental tissues (n=10).

claim: CALHM2, CALHM4, and CALHM6 are upregulated during trophoblast differentiation.
source: By transcript analysis, we found the paralogs CALHM2, 4, and 6 to be highly expressed in this organ and upregulated during trophoblast differentiation.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data in Figure 1B showing marked upregulation of CALHM2, 4, and 6 during differentiation from cytotrophoblasts to syncytiotrophoblasts (n=5).

claim: CALHM4 shows the most pronounced upregulation during trophoblast differentiation.
source: We found marked upregulation of CALHM2, 4 and 6 during differentiation, which was most pronounced for CALHM4 (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B comparing cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast stages.

claim: CALHM4 forms decameric and undecameric assemblies.
source: Cryo-EM structures of CALHM4 display decameric and undecameric assemblies with large cylindrical pore
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM structural data showing both 10-mer and 11-mer assemblies of CALHM4 at resolutions of 4.07 Å and 3.69 Å respectively, as shown in Figure 3A and Figure 4.

claim: CALHM4 has a large cylindrical pore.
source: Cryo-EM structures of CALHM4 display decameric and undecameric assemblies with large cylindrical pore
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM structural data and pore radius calculations shown in Figure 6A, demonstrating a cylindrical pore geometry.

claim: CALHM6 has a conical pore that narrows at the intracellular side.
source: while in CALHM6 a conformational change has converted the pore shape into a conus that narrows at the intracellular side, thus describing distinct functional states of the channel.
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 7, demonstrating the conical pore geometry of CALHM6.

claim: Lipids occupy the cylindrical pore of CALHM4 in a bilayer-like arrangement.
source: The pore geometry alters the distribution of lipids, which occupy the cylindrical pore of CALHM4 in a bilayer-like arrangement
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM density analysis shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, showing bimodal density distribution consistent with lipid bilayer organization.

claim: Lipids have redistributed in the conical pore of CALHM6.
source: whereas they have redistributed in the conical pore of CALHM6 with potential functional consequences.
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM density analysis shown in Figure 7H, demonstrating altered lipid density distribution compared to CALHM4.

claim: CALHM1 is activated by depolarization and a decrease in extracellular Ca2+ concentration.
source: CALHM1, the currently best characterized paralog, forms ion channels that are activated by depolarization and a decrease in the extracellular Ca2+-concentration (Ma et al., 2012; Taruno et al., 2013b)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ma et al., 2012; Taruno et al., 2013b) and confirmed by electrophysiology data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CALHM1 mutations are associated with increased risk for late-onset Alzheimer's disease.
source: with mutations being associated with an increased risk for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (Dreses-Werringloer et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dreses-Werringloer et al., 2008.

claim: CALHM1 forms heteromers with CALHM3 in a physiological context.
source: Although functional on its own (Ma et al., 2012), in a physiological context CALHM1 probably forms heteromers with the subunit CALHM3 (Ma et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ma et al., 2018b.

claim: CALHM1/CALHM3 heteromeric channels play an important role in sweet, bitter and umami taste reception.
source: These heteromeric channels play an important role as secondary receptors for sweet, bitter and umami taste reception in type II taste bud cells by catalyzing the non-vesicular release of ATP (Ma et al., 2018b; Taruno et al., 2013a; Taruno et al., 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2018b; Taruno et al., 2013a; Taruno et al., 2013b.

claim: CALHM2 is ubiquitously expressed and mediates ATP release in astrocytes.
source: A second paralog with an assigned physiological role is CALHM2, which is ubiquitously expressed and was proposed to mediate ATP release in astrocytes (Ma et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ma et al., 2018a.

claim: CALHM2 assembles into undecameric channels.
source: CALHM2 was found to assemble into undecameric channels, which in certain cases dimerize via contacts on the extracellular side in an assembly that resembles gap-junctions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies (Choi et al., 2019; Syrjanen et al., 2020) and confirmed by 2D class averages in Figure 3C.

claim: CALHM1 shows an octameric organization.
source: In contrast to CALHM2 channels, the structure of CALHM1 shows a smaller octameric organization (Demura et al., 2020; Syrjanen et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Demura et al., 2020; Syrjanen et al., 2020.

claim: CALHM proteins are not structurally related to connexins and VRACs despite predictions.
source: Although predicted to be related to connexins and volume-regulated anion channels (VRACs) of the LRRC8 family (Siebert et al., 2013), the four membrane-spanning helices of the CALHM subunit exhibit a distinct arrangement, which refutes a common structural ancestry between these protein families (Choi et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Choi et al., 2019 and structural comparison shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: CALHM2, CALHM4, and CALHM6 do not show pronounced activity under conditions where CALHM1 channels are open.
source: A systematic comparative functional characterization by electrophysiology did not reveal pronounced activity of either of these paralogs under conditions where CALHM1 channels are open
evidence: The claim is supported by two-electrode voltage-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: CALHM2, CALHM4, and CALHM6 might be regulated by different and currently unknown mechanisms compared to CALHM1.
source: thus suggesting that the former might be regulated by different and currently unknown mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of activity under CALHM1-activating conditions shown in Figure 2, suggesting different regulatory mechanisms.

claim: The syncytiotrophoblast layer constitutes a tight diffusion barrier in the placenta.
source: While endothelial cells lining the fetal vessels allow to a certain extent diffusion of (small) molecules through paracellular pathways (Edwards et al., 1993; Lewis et al., 2013), the STB layer constitutes a tight diffusion barrier.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Edwards et al., 1993; Lewis et al., 2013.

claim: Syncytiotrophoblasts are polarized multinucleated cells with apical side towards maternal blood and basal side towards fetal capillaries.
source: STB are polarized multinucleated cells presenting their apical side towards the maternal blood and their basal side towards the fetal capillaries.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of placental anatomy.

claim: The targeted expression of receptors, channels or transport proteins of the STB determines the directionality of transport across the placenta.
source: Hence, the targeted expression of receptors, channels or transport proteins of the STB determines the directionality of transport across the placenta, which is essential for the adequate development of the fetus (Lager and Powell, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lager and Powell, 2012.

claim: CALHM family members function as non-selective channels permeable to large substances such as ATP.
source: In humans, the CALHM family encompasses six paralogs, some of which function as non-selective channels that are permeable to large substances such as ATP (Ma et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ma et al., 2016.

claim: All three placental CALHM paralogs (2, 4, 6) are expressed and targeted to the plasma membrane of X. laevis oocytes.
source: To detect proteins in the plasma membrane, we have used a surface-biotinylation approach and found all placental paralogs to be expressed and targeted at high levels to the surface of oocytes at the time of the measurement (i.e. 40–60 hr after injection of mRNA) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by surface biotinylation western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CALHM1 shows slowly activating currents at positive voltage in the presence of millimolar Ca2+ concentrations.
source: In our studies, we were able to reproduce the functional hallmarks of CALHM1, which are manifested in the absence of currents at negative voltage and slowly activating currents at positive voltage at millimolar concentrations of extracellular Ca2+
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: CALHM1 shows a strong increase of currents upon Ca2+ removal in the entire voltage range.
source: and a strong increase of currents upon Ca2+ removal in the entire voltage range (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Currents of CALHM2, 4, and 6 are within the range of endogenous currents of X. laevis oocytes.
source: In contrast to CALHM1, the current response of homomeric CALHM2, 4, and 6 channels was generally small and within the range of endogenous currents of X. laevis oocytes not expressing any of the proteins (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data comparing CALHM2, 4, 6 to negative control oocytes in Figure 2B.

claim: CALHM2, 4, and 6 currents show no pronounced voltage-dependence.
source: These currents neither showed pronounced voltage-dependence nor were they altered by Ca2+-removal in a statistically significant manner (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2B-D showing no significant rectification.

claim: CALHM2, 4, and 6 currents are not significantly altered by Ca2+ removal.
source: These currents neither showed pronounced voltage-dependence nor were they altered by Ca2+-removal in a statistically significant manner (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2B-D showing no significant change upon Ca2+ removal.

claim: All three placental paralogs expressed high levels of protein in HEK293 cells.
source: For a biochemical and structural characterization of placental CALHM channels, we have expressed constructs coding for human CALHM2, 4 and 6 in HEK293 cells. In contrast to the poor yields obtained for human CALHM1, all three placental paralogs expressed high levels of protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by FSEC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and successful purification for cryo-EM.

claim: CALHM4 and CALHM6 form assemblies containing between 10 and 12 subunits.
source: As expected from the size-exclusion profiles, all paralogs form large and heterogenic multimeric assemblies containing between 10 and 12 subunits.
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data processing showing decameric and undecameric assemblies in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplements 2-4.

claim: The vast majority of CALHM6 oligomeric channels do not interact with each other.
source: Whereas in the CALHM6 sample a vast majority of these oligomeric channels do not interact (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 4)
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM micrographs and 2D class averages shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Almost complete dimerization was found for CALHM4.
source: we have found almost complete dimerization for CALHM4 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3)
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data showing paired CALHM4 channels in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplements 2-3.

claim: A significant fraction of CALHM2 particles dimerize.
source: and a significant fraction of particles to dimerize in case of CALHM2 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by 2D class averages shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: CALHM4 channel pairing proceeds via contacts at the intracellular side.
source: Unlike to previous reports of CALHM2 structures, where interactions between channels were mediated by extracellular loops (Choi et al., 2019; Syrjanen et al., 2020), the pairing in the CALHM4 sample proceeds via contacts at the intracellular side (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CALHM4 forms cylindrical pores.
source: We also observed two distinct protein conformations in our data with CALHM4 and CALHM6 channels forming cylindrical and conical pores, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3D and Figure 4.

claim: CALHM6 forms conical pores.
source: We also observed two distinct protein conformations in our data with CALHM4 and CALHM6 channels forming cylindrical and conical pores, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 3D and Figure 7.

claim: The structural properties of CALHM4 are not affected by the presence or absence of Ca2+.
source: For the determination of the CALHM4 structure, we have recorded cryo-EM data in the presence and absence of Ca2+ and observed similar structural properties in both samples, which are not affected by divalent cations (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of cryo-EM structures from datasets with and without Ca2+ shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: CALHM4 decamers have a resolution of 4.1 Å and undecamers have a resolution of 3.7 Å.
source: The cryo-EM density of the decamers extends to a resolution of 4.1 Å and undecamers to 3.7 Å, which in both cases permitted the unambiguous interpretation by an atomic model (Figure 3—figure supplements 2, 3 and 5A, Video 1, Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by FSC curves and resolution estimates shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3, and Table 1.

claim: CALHM4 channels form approximately 90 Å high cylindrical proteins that span the lipid bilayer.
source: The CALHM4 channels form approximately 90 Å high cylindrical proteins that span the lipid bilayer with regions at their respective periphery extending into the aqueous environment on either side of the membrane (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 4.

claim: Decameric CALHM4 channels have dimensions of 110 Å in the plane of the membrane.
source: In the plane of the membrane, the dimensions of decameric and undecameric CALHM4 channels amount to 110 Å and 120 Å respectively (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural measurements shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Undecameric CALHM4 channels have dimensions of 120 Å in the plane of the membrane.
source: In the plane of the membrane, the dimensions of decameric and undecameric CALHM4 channels amount to 110 Å and 120 Å respectively (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural measurements shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Individual subunits in decameric and undecameric CALHM4 assemblies show equivalent conformations.
source: Irrespective of their distinct oligomerization, the individual subunits in both assemblies show equivalent conformations, which resemble the recently described structures of CALHM1 and 2 (Choi et al., 2019; Demura et al., 2020; Syrjanen et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison of subunits from decameric and undecameric assemblies and citations to previous structures.

claim: The CALHM subunit organization is likely general for the CALHM family.
source: and thus define an organization that is likely general for the CALHM family (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from structural similarity across CALHM paralogs shown in Figure 5A and sequence alignment in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The transmembrane helices in CALHM channels are arranged in an anticlockwise manner when viewed from the extracellular side.
source: When viewed from the extracellular side, the transmembrane helices in connexin, innexin and VRAC channels (Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Maeda et al., 2009; Oshima et al., 2016) are arranged in a clockwise manner, whereas the arrangement in CALHM channels is anticlockwise (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5B,C and citations to connexin, innexin, and VRAC structures.

claim: The four helices of connexin and related channels form a tightly interacting left-handed bundle with oval cross-section.
source: Moreover, in connexins and related channels, the four helices form a tightly interacting left-handed bundle with a common core, resulting in a structure with an oval cross-section (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The helices of the CALHM subunit are organized as two layers conferring a trapezoid cross-section.
source: Conversely, the helices of the CALHM subunit are organized as two layers conferring an overall trapezoid cross-section (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Connexins and LRRC8 channels form hexamers.
source: Finally, whereas connexins and LRRC8 channels form hexamers, and innexins form octamers, an oligomeric arrangement that has also been observed for CALHM1, the larger CALHM4 channels contain either 10 or 11 subunits (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of connexin and LRRC8 channel structures.

claim: Innexins form octamers.
source: Finally, whereas connexins and LRRC8 channels form hexamers, and innexins form octamers, an oligomeric arrangement that has also been observed for CALHM1, the larger CALHM4 channels contain either 10 or 11 subunits (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of innexin channel structures.

claim: The outer layer of the CALHM subunit is composed of interacting α-helices TM2-4.
source: The outer layer of the CALHM subunit is composed of the interacting α-helices TM2-4, which are arranged in one row sharing mutual interactions only with their respective neighbor.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The inner layer of the CALHM subunit consists of TM1, which exclusively interacts with TM3.
source: The inner layer consists of TM1, which on its entire length exclusively interacts with TM3, the central helix of the outer layer (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: TM1 helices forming the inner layer are distant from each other and not involved in mutual inter-subunit interactions.
source: In contrast, the respective TM1 helices forming the inner layer are distant from each other and thus not involved in mutual inter-subunit interactions (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: The N-terminus of CALHM4 forms a helix (NH) oriented perpendicular to TM1 parallel to the membrane plane.
source: In the region preceding TM1, the residues of the N-terminus form a helix (NH) that is oriented perpendicular to the first transmembrane segment parallel to the plane of the lipid bilayer (Figure 4, Figure 5D, Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4, Figure 5D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The conformations of NH and TM1 are best defined in CALHM4 among family members of known structures.
source: Among the family members of known structures, the conformations of NH and TM1 are best defined in CALHM4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A), whereas weaker density of these fragments in the equivalent state of CALHM1 and 2 points towards a higher mobility of this region in latter proteins (Choi et al., 2019; Syrjanen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of cryo-EM density quality shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and citations to CALHM1 and 2 structures.

claim: The extracellular domain of CALHM4 contains two conserved disulfide bridges.
source: Both segments of the extracellular domain are stabilized by two conserved disulfide bridges (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The CTH-helices form a 30 Å-high intracellular ring by mutual interaction with neighboring subunits.
source: By mutual interaction with neighboring subunits, the CTH-helices form a 30 Å-high intracellular ring that extends from the membrane into the cytoplasm (Figures 4 and 5A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 4, 5A, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The C-terminal loops mediate the bulk of the interaction relating CALHM4 channel pairs.
source: In this way the C-terminal loops mediate the bulk of the interaction relating CALHM4 channel pairs in an arrangement whose relevance in a cellular context is still ambiguous.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The diameter of CALHM4 pore at both entrances measures about 52 Å for decamers and 60 Å for undecamers.
source: The diameter at both entrances of the pore measures about 52 Å and 60 Å for decameric and undecameric assemblies respectively, thus defining the properties of an unusually large channel, which could be permeable to molecular substrates (Figure 6A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by pore radius calculations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At the constriction, decameric CALHM4 channels are about 20 Å wide.
source: Even at the constriction located at the intracellular membrane leaflet where the respective N-terminal helices NH project towards the pore axis, the decameric channels are about 20 Å and undecameric channels 30 Å wide (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by pore radius calculations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: At the constriction, undecameric CALHM4 channels are about 30 Å wide.
source: Even at the constriction located at the intracellular membrane leaflet where the respective N-terminal helices NH project towards the pore axis, the decameric channels are about 20 Å and undecameric channels 30 Å wide (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by pore radius calculations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The CALHM4 pore would be sufficiently large to accommodate an ATP molecule.
source: In both cases the pore would thus be sufficiently large to accommodate an ATP molecule, consistent with the notion of CALHM proteins forming ATP-permeable channels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from pore dimensions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E and comparison to ATP size.

claim: The large pore size of CALHM4 contrasts with the lack of appreciable currents in electrophysiology.
source: Remarkably, this large pore size is in sharp contrast to our functional characterization by electrophysiology where we did not observe appreciable currents for CALHM4 (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of structural data (Figure 6A) with electrophysiology data (Figure 2A).

claim: The absence of activating or presence of inhibiting components might impede ion conduction in CALHM4.
source: which suggests that either the absence of activating or presence of inhibiting components might impede ion conduction.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the discrepancy between large pore size and lack of currents.

claim: The pore of CALHM4 is highly hydrophobic at the membrane core region.
source: Due to the prevalence of aliphatic residues lining the pore at the assumed location of the membrane core, the pore is highly hydrophobic, whereas the regions extending into the aqueous environment contain polar and charged residues (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical property analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The side of the helical N-terminus facing the membrane at the intracellular boundary is hydrophobic.
source: Similarly, the side of the helical N-terminus, which faces the membrane at its intracellular boundary, is hydrophobic (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Layered density distribution inside the CALHM4 pore matches properties of lipid membranes.
source: This density is observed with similar properties in decameric and undecameric proteins in both datasets of CALHM4 obtained in either absence or presence of Ca2+ (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C). Its distribution displays features that quantitatively match the corresponding properties of lipid membranes obtained from a comparison to cryo-EM density of liposomes and computer simulations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by density analysis shown in Figure 6D and comparison to simulations in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Phospholipids commonly found in HEK cell membranes were detected in the CALHM4 sample by mass spectrometry.
source: We thus analyzed the composition of small molecules that are co-purified with CALHM4 by mass spectrometry and were able to detect phospholipids that are commonly found in the membranes of HEK cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The data are compatible with the presence of a lipid bilayer within the pore region of CALHM4 channels.
source: Collectively, our data are compatible with the presence of a lipid bilayer located within the pore region of CALHM4 channels, which could interfere with the diffusion of charged substances.
evidence: The claim is inferred from cryo-EM density distribution, mass spectrometry data, and comparison to membrane simulations.

claim: It is unclear whether the CALHM4 structure defines a conductive conformation or a conformation with membrane-like assembly impeding ion conduction.
source: Thus, despite of its large pore diameter, it is at this point unclear whether the CALHM4 structure defines a conductive conformation of CALHM channel or alternatively a conformation that harbors a membrane-like assembly residing inside the pore that would impede ion conduction.
evidence: The claim reflects uncertainty in functional interpretation based on structural and functional data.

claim: CALHM6 data shows a heterogeneous distribution of decameric and undecameric channels with prevalence of decamers (60%).
source: As in case of CALHM4, data of CALHM6 shows a heterogeneous distribution of decameric and undecameric channels, but in this case with a prevalence of the former amounting to 60% of the classified particles (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM data processing shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Decameric and undecameric CALHM6 assemblies contain subunits with equivalent conformations.
source: Both assemblies of CALHM6 contain subunits with equivalent conformations, which are better defined in the smaller oligomers (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison of decameric and undecameric CALHM6.

claim: The decameric CALHM6 structure has a resolution of 4.4 Å.
source: Unlike CALHM4, the lower resolution of the CALHM6 density of 4.4 Å, precludes a detailed interpretation of the structure for all parts of the protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by FSC curves shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4D.

claim: There is no dimerization of CALHM6 channels.
source: Unlike CALHM4, there is no dimerization of CALHM6 channels and the C-terminal region following the cytoplasmic helix CTH instead appears to engage in intramolecular interactions with the outside of the cytoplasmic rim for most of its length (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 7A and Figure 3B.

claim: In CALHM6, there is a slight expansion of the protein parallel to the membrane and moderate contraction in perpendicular direction compared to CALHM4.
source: Upon comparison of decameric channels of both paralogs, in CALHM6 we find a slight expansion of the protein parallel to the membrane and an accompanying moderate contraction in perpendicular direction (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural superposition shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In CALHM6, TM1 has detached from TM3 and moved by 60° towards the pore axis.
source: These differences are most pronounced for TM1, which in CALHM6 has detached from TM3 and moved by 60° towards the pore axis around a hinge located upstream of a conserved phenylalanine at the end of TM1 (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 7B-E.

claim: The conformation of the proximal loop connecting TM1 and 2 is stabilized by two conserved cysteines involved in disulfide bridges.
source: In both structures, the conformation of the proximal loop connecting TM1 and 2 is stabilized by two conserved cysteines, which are involved in disulfide bridges with the region connecting TM3 and TM4 (Figure 7F–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 7F-G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The intracellular half of TM3 tilts away from the pore axis by 30° around a pivot near a conserved proline residue.
source: As a consequence of the disruption of its interaction with TM1, the intracellular halve of TM3 tilts away from the pore axis by 30° around a pivot located close to a conserved proline residue (P115 in CALHM4), which probably destabilizes the helix (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: The transition from cylindrical to conical conformation is accompanied by dissociation of interactions between TM1 and TM3.
source: The transition from a conformation observed in CALHM4 to a conformation defined by CALHM6 is accompanied by the dissociation of interactions between TM1 and 3, which are mediated by conserved residues involving a cluster of hydrophobic interactions at the extracellular side and additional interactions on the entire length of both α-helices (Figure 7F–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D, Video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 7F-G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The iris-like movement of TM1 converts a cylindrical pore to a funnel which narrows towards the intracellular side.
source: When viewed from the outside this transition thus resembles the closing of an aperture and it converts a cylindrical pore to a funnel which narrows towards the intracellular side while creating a large cavity between TM1 and TM3 that becomes accessible from the cytoplasm (Figure 7C, Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 7C and Video 3.

claim: TM1 in CALHM6 is less well defined compared to the rest of the protein, reflecting increased flexibility.
source: In the cryo-EM density, TM1 is less well defined compared to the rest of the protein reflecting its increased flexibility in the observed structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cryo-EM density quality shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The distribution of pore density in CALHM6 is comparable to CALHM2 in complex with ruthenium red.
source: A comparable distribution of pore density is found in the structure of CALHM2 in complex with ruthenium red, which resides in a similar conical pore conformation (Choi et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published CALHM2 structure (Choi et al., 2019).

claim: The functional assignment of the CALHM6 structure remains ambiguous despite conformational differences to CALHM4.
source: Thus, despite the pronounced conformational differences to CALHM4 and the fact that the CALHM6 structure appears to contain features of a closed pore, a definitive functional assignment remains also in this case ambiguous.
evidence: The claim reflects uncertainty in functional interpretation based on structural features.

claim: The concentrations of CALHM mRNAs are high in comparison to other transport proteins in the placenta.
source: In all cases, the concentrations of the respective CALHM mRNAs are high in comparison to other transport proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) suggesting their involvement in important placenta-related membrane transport processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data comparing CALHM paralogs to other transport proteins shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dimerization of CALHM4 might be a consequence of interactions formed between solubilized proteins.
source: This observation further supports the notion that the dimerization of CALHM4 might be a consequence of interactions formed between solubilized proteins where the mobile C-terminus could equally well engage in intra- and intermolecular interactions, of which the latter would be multiplied in the highly symmetric arrangement.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on comparison of CALHM4 and CALHM6 C-terminal interactions.

claim: The smaller size of CALHM1 channels could be responsible for its functional properties manifested in electrophysiological recordings.
source: In this respect, the smaller size of CALHM1 channels could be responsible for its functional properties, which are manifested in electrophysiological recordings.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning connecting oligomeric state to functional properties.

claim: The low current response of CALHM2, 4, and 6 likely reflects their low open probability.
source: The low current response contrasts with the larger oligomeric organization of these proteins, which should lead to channels of even higher conductance than observed for CALHM1, and thus likely reflects their low open probability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the discrepancy between large pore size and low currents.

claim: It remains puzzling how the large pores of CALHM channels can be regulated to prevent leakage under resting conditions.
source: In that respect it remains puzzling how the large pores observed for the investigated structures (with diameters of CALHM4 decamers exceeding 40 Å within the membrane and 20 Å at the respective constriction, Figure 6A) can be regulated to prevent leakage of substances under resting conditions, which would be deleterious to the cell.
evidence: The claim reflects an unresolved question based on structural observations.

claim: The cylindrical pore conformation of CALHM4 was previously assigned to an open state.
source: In this previous study, the cylindrical conformation was assigned to an open state and the conical conformation to a closed state of the pore, a proposal that is further supported by a structure of the bound blocker rubidium red which appears to stabilize the conical conformation (Choi et al., 2019; Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Choi et al., 2019.

claim: The conical pore conformation was previously assigned to a closed state.
source: In this previous study, the cylindrical conformation was assigned to an open state and the conical conformation to a closed state of the pore, a proposal that is further supported by a structure of the bound blocker rubidium red which appears to stabilize the conical conformation (Choi et al., 2019; Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Choi et al., 2019.

claim: Ruthenium red appears to stabilize the conical conformation of CALHM2.
source: a proposal that is further supported by a structure of the bound blocker rubidium red which appears to stabilize the conical conformation (Choi et al., 2019; Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Choi et al., 2019.

claim: There are puzzling questions that prevent definitive assignment of pore conformations to functional states.
source: While, at first glance, the relationship between observed pore conformations and their corresponding functional states appears evident, there are still puzzling questions which prevent a definitive assignment at this stage.
evidence: The claim reflects uncertainty in functional interpretation.

claim: The presence of lipids within the pore offers a potential alternative mechanism for regulation of CALHM channels.
source: In that respect, the presence of lipids within the pore of large CALHM channels is noteworthy as it offers a potential alternative mechanism for regulation.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on observed lipid density in the pore.

claim: Two alternative scenarios for regulation in large CALHM channels are possible: protein gate or lipid gate.
source: We thus could envision two alternative scenarios which might underly regulation in large CALHM channels where the gate in the closed state could either be formed by part of the protein or by lipids (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim presents hypothetical models shown in Figure 8.

claim: Both protein gate and lipid gate models are hypothetical at this stage.
source: Both models are at this stage hypothetical and it is still unclear how lipids in the pore would rearrange during activation.
evidence: The claim acknowledges the speculative nature of the proposed models.

claim: It is unclear whether pairwise interactions of CALHM channels are of relevance in a physiological context.
source: Although intriguing, it is currently unclear whether any of the observed pairwise interactions is of relevance in a physiological context.
evidence: The claim reflects uncertainty about the biological significance of observed channel dimers.

claim: Human placental tissues were collected from healthy term pregnancies following elective cesarean section beyond 37 weeks of gestation.
source: Placentas were collected from uncomplicated pregnancies following elective cesarean section beyond 37 weeks of gestation without prior labor upon patients request or due to breech presentation.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental sample collection procedure.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis using cytokeratin 7 was performed to assure purity of isolated trophoblast cells.
source: In order to assure the purity of the cells, flow cytometry analysis was performed by using the trophoblast-specific epithelial cell marker cytokeratin 7 (Maldonado-Estrada et al., 2004) (anti-cytokeratin 7, Dako, Switzerland).
evidence: The claim describes the quality control method for cell isolation with citation to Maldonado-Estrada et al., 2004.

claim: Vimentin served as a negative marker for potentially contaminating cells in trophoblast isolation.
source: Vimentin (anti-vimentin, Sigma, USA), which is only expressed in potentially contaminating cells (e.g. mesenchymal cells, fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, stromal cells) served as a negative marker (Soares and Hunt, 2006).
evidence: The claim describes the quality control method with citation to Soares and Hunt, 2006.

claim: The cryo-EM density maps and atomic models have been deposited in public databases.
source: The cryo-EM density maps of CALHM4 in absence of Ca2+ and CALHM4 and CALHM6 in presence of Ca2+ have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank under following ID codes: EMD-10917, EMD-10919, EMD-10920, EMD-10921, EMD-10924 and EMD-10925. The coordinates of the corresponding atomic models of CALHM4 and CALHM6 have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank under ID codes 6YTK, 6YTL, 6YTO, 6YTQ, 6YTV and 6YTX.
evidence: The claim provides accession codes for data deposition.
